entities.name: Imelda Lambertini
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Blessed Imelda Lambertini (c. 1322 – May 12, 1333) was an Italian Catholic mystic and a profound exemplar of eucharistic devotion in the late Medieval period, revered for her precocious spiritual intensity and her miraculous death during her first communion. Born into the noble Lambertini family of Bologna, her brief life, though obscure in its specifics, became a powerful narrative within the Dominican Order and the broader Catholic Church, shaping practices of early communion and inspiring countless young devotees. She represents a significant, albeit niche, aspect of medieval piety, emphasizing personal mystical experience at a tender age in a time when such experiences were often reserved for adult ascetics.

From a very young age, Imelda demonstrated an extraordinary piety, reportedly expressing a deep longing to receive the Eucharist. Despite her fervent desire, the standard practice in the 14th century was to delay First Communion until a more mature age, typically around 12-14 years old. According to hagiographic accounts, on May 12, 1333, while attending Mass at the Dominican convent of Val di Pietra in Bologna, a miraculous host is said to have descended from the altar and hovered above her head. Following this sign, the officiating priest administered the sacrament, and Imelda reportedly died immediately thereafter, overcome by spiritual ecstasy. This extraordinary event, witnessed by other nuns and clergy, solidified her reputation for sanctity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Imelda Lambertini holds significant regional and thematic importance, primarily for her posthumous influence on the Catholic Church's practices regarding First Communion, directly informing Pope Pius X's decree that lowered the age for receiving the Eucharist for millions worldwide.
